projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Raymond E. Tuwalski was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Raymond E. Tuwalski. Ray served in the U.S. Army Air Corps with the Second Bomb Group in Italy and the Ninth Bomb Group in the Philippines. His highest rank was major at retirement from the Air Force Reserve. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Tuwalski's home in East Lake, Ohio on February 13th, 2002. Ray was 80 at the time of this recording. You said you had some memories of Pearl Harbor that you wanted to share.

sp.speaker: Raymond E. Tuwalski
sp.p: The only memories I'd have of Pearl Harbor is just as anyone who was in this country -- was totally shocked when it did occur. And I knew that the die was cast and what the future would hold for me; that is that I would soon be serving my country. But I was not yet 21 years of age when this occurred. I wouldn't be until 1942 in July. So I approached my parents and I said that I want to join up. But they would not hear anything of it, so I stewed about it for a few weeks and time went on. And so sometime around February, why, I was at downtown Cleveland and I happened to see a placard in a public square about the Air Force Cadets, so I went into the Federal Building and went to the recruiting office and inquired about it. And so he said, Yes.

You can get into the Cadets but you have to be 21, or otherwise ya'll have to have the signatures of your parents allowing you to enroll into the program. I said, I don't know if I can do this sort of thing because my parents are steadfast in their minds, No, you're not going. I said, But -- I spoke to my parents. I said, Lordy, another few months down the road a piece or halfway down the road I will be able to go because I'll be 21. But by then the Draft Board is going to get into me, and I want to choose what line of service I want to be in. But they still would not sign those papers.

So I went back to the sergeant and told him, I'm having problems. Well, he said, Tell you what, son, how about I make arrangements and the next class that's going to be coming through for exams -- these are written exams. I looked at him and I said, Well, what takes place then? He said, You'll have the written exams. At least if you can get past the -- if you make it, that's great. Then you've passed that hurdle. And if you don't make it, then well, then you'll know what's going to take place thereafter.

So I said, Hey, that's okay by me. Which is exactly what I did. And I was really nervous because when I got in that classroom, there must have been about 30 guys in that room. And the sergeant comes in, this is another one, comes in and he really hits us below the belt when he says, you know, you've got 30 some odd people in here, but I doubt whether more than ten of you are going to pass this exam. Wow, I was only a high school graduate at the time. But I did have the exam and later on within that week I got notification that I had passed the exam. And so I got my piece of paper and I went right back down to Public Square and I said, What do I do now, Sarge? He looks at me and says, Well, you're still going to have to wait son, or otherwise convince your parents that you should be getting in. So all right.

I went back to my parents again and I showed them. I said look, Pop, Mom, I passed. And, no, we're not going -- my mom said, No. We're not going to sign that paper. I said for God's sake. We're talking this is March now already and July I will be 21. No way, Jose. So I stood it out and -- but on July 27th, which was my 21st birthday, I'd already talked to the sergeant about that and he said, Well, we'll have a medical officer around here to check you out. And I did go there and I got checked out et cetera, and I got stamped that I was clear.

And at that time I was engaged to what is my precious wife and so to celebrate I called her. She was working at GE at the time. I called her and told her that I had made it and we're going out tonight. And we really did. I took her to Lanna-Co's (phonetic) which is right in Play-O (phonetic) Square. Restaurant no longer exists. But it was an elegant restaurant. The center was a dance floor. It was a string orchestra that played there, marvelous music. The tables were all along the wall through the peripheral of the room. We had a marvelous evening. But that's how I celebrated my entry into the Cadets.

Now, this is July 27th when I passed the exam. August 5th I was enrolled into the service, but I did not get going -- get into active duty. I had -- they had to have a slot for me. I had no idea how the Cadet program was. But in January, early January of 1943 I got the orders, and I was -- I got shipped over to Fort Hayes, Columbus.

I met a young man from Columbus, Lowell Tope, and he and I stuck together like glue for most of the year because everything in the service is always alphabetical. He's a Tope, T-o-p-e, and I'm a Tuwalski, T-u-w. And so we were always bunked next to one another throughout.

And so from Fort Hayes we were shipped to Nashville, Tennessee. A horrible place, but I was -- we were placed in casual, maybe because we were civilians and that's an Army base, why, they kept -- was casual. They kept you quarantined, so to speak, from everyone else in the camp. I'd like to digress and get back again -- the orders were that when we were to be shipped to Nashville -- as a matter of fact, even before I got there when we were going to Columbus, I -- there was a letter, advisory letter saying, Make sure that you have clothing, change of clothing, tooth brush, tooth paste, shaving cream, et cetera, to last for at least a two-week period of time.

I did -- I had -- my duffel bag was full. It would take care of all of my needs. However, there were some cadets in there that came there with nothing. And we'd just got settled in the indoor barracks and a young lad in uniform came by, a corporal, his name was Smith. And this was in the evening. And he offered since we were not able -- we did not have access to any place else in the camp, why, he offered that he would get anything that we required.

So there was some guys that they needed just about everything. So he has a laundry list. He writes down a list of names and et cetera, and he approximates about how much it's going to cost. It's going to cost less than you can get it in town being you're at a post exchange. And so all right. These guys come across with the green backs, hand it all over to him. And I'll say this much for him, he did come back and he got everything that everyone wanted and they all got change and all that bit.

So in about two weeks we were out of casual and were roaming around through the camp waiting for assignment to the next place we were going to go. Which by the way, my first year in the service is going to read like a travel log from the various camps that I was bouncing around, bouncing around through. So we all go to the PX. What an enlightenment it was for these fellows that used Snuffy--we called him Snuffy Smith when we used his service--because they saw the prices, and they discovered what they'd shelled out -- the money they'd shelled out for what they got. But they couldn't find Snuffy Smith anywhere in camp.

But after that, why, -- and in the meantime I got sicker than a dog because I caught what is known as Nashville-gitis. That camp was about the worst area in Nashville that you ever wanted to see. And so many of us got it. You lost your voice and your throat swelled up. And I was about ready to go -- to be held back because they wanted to remove my tonsils but they couldn't remove my tonsils because they were so swollen. But you had to agree to the operation and I said no.

And I was glad I did because when we left and we were assigned into Maxwell Field in Montgomery, Alabama in about two weeks, why, I was just cleared because the climate was entirely different; all that sunshine, palm trees and, et cetera. Maxwell Field, that was a pre-flight school and there was again a weeding out period there, because there's intensive training, a lot of classroom work. And if you don't make it, you're gone. They send you somewhere else. And it was then that I did make it.

And just prior to leaving there, why, there was what's called a Cadet Ball that took place on April 28th of 1943. I had arranged -- if you had a date with -- if someone has a date to the Cadet Ball, why, they invited you to do this. So I had saved up quite a few bucks and I called Dorothy, my present wife, and I asked her if she could get the time off to go, maybe vacation time or something. So she got the message back to me that, yes, she could make it, and so I arranged for the train fare. And at the same time through the U.S.O. I was introduced then to an address in Montgomery and to a name. I went and visited the home. It was the Richbergs. Introduced myself and inquired whether they would take Dorothy in during the time that we had this Cadet Ball. And they looked me over and figured I must be an honest Joe and all of that, but they agreed to it and so I put the bucks down for her as well.

Now, she was due to arrive at a certain time and date. I had a message -- and they said that they would go to the train station and they would pick her up and bring her in. Well, then I got this frantic message from the Richbergs, Where's Dorothy? The train isn't in. What's happening?

And here it was just at that cotton picking time when our President Roosevelt decided to take a trip down to Maxwell Field to review us, and there we were standing in parade and in review. And Roosevelt goes by sitting in his limo and he reviews the cadet class going through. We're standing out there right there at the tarmac of the airport. So what had happened was that the train that Dorothy was on was pushed over on the siding, held over for about six or eight hours and et cetera. So poor Dorothy got into Montgomery -- you know what, she didn't know that anybody was going to be there, but thank God for the Richbergs. They were there for her.

Fortunately Mr. Richberg happened to work for the railroad company so he knew what the situation was, because his wife was the one that was frantic about it; but he knew what went on and so he had told her to get over there about this time and you'll be able to pick her up. So that's what happened at that particular time.

I moved ahead a little too fast. I wanted to mention something about Nashville. We got -- after we got through casual in Nashville, why, we got an opportunity to go into town, and I got -- took the bus into Nashville. I wanted to see all of Nashville, so we took the buses from camp to the heart of town. This was a campus. But then once I got into town, I wanted to explore Nashville, so I got on a street car. I get on this thing and I walk through -- and I liked to sit in the back end of a street car back home, so I made a left-hand turn, walked all the way into the back end of the street car.

People were looking at me. They figured this guy's got to be a yank because there's a color line on the street car from the floor all the way up the side of the walls, up the roof and back down into the floor again. And anything which is down towards the back end of the street car, that's where the blacks sat at that time and the rest is for the whites. And I'm sitting there amongst all the blacks. But I soon realize what I had done. I just felt very uneasy about it all, just to see this color line because I came up here from the north.
Heck, I played with blacks and I was friends with them and all. I -- that was a revelation to me.

After graduation from Maxwell, well, then I was sent to Union City, Tennessee for pilot training. I should state at this time that I did not want to be a pilot. I wanted to be a navigator in the Cadet Program. My thoughts were always, hey, a pilot -- if I get into a bomber or any other aircraft, the pilot is nothing more than a taxi driver. I wanted to be a navigator and tell the pilot where to go. So that was one of the reasons why I wanted to be a navigator.

But nevertheless, they said, No. You'll make a good pilot. So I went up there in Embry-Riddle Field, Union City, Tennessee and -- well, I washed out of there. It was noted on my reports that there was lack of progress. So maybe I wasn't too bright of an individual, I suppose. But be that as it may, I took no offense at it and I ended up back again at Nashville Cadet, the very same Army depo that I had been taken to when I left Fort Hayes Columbus. All right. I'm with these guys. We're just waiting for a new assignment.

Back into town we go carousing around a bit. And this one particular late afternoon we were going -- riding this bus heading back into town, but who in the world is sitting on that bus but Snuffy Smith. And I recall -- it's so vivid to me because when that bus is heading in towards the camp there was a -- like a dead end almost you could say, but there was a right-hand 90 degree left-hand turn in the road. And just at that particular turn in the road, why, there's a huge monument depicting about some Civil War skirmish or whatever had taken place, a huge monument there.

Some of these guys, they had remembered Snuffy Smith. They ripped him off of that bus right at that point. They knew it wasn't too far away from the entrance of the camp when they did this. And they beat the living hell out of him right then and there. They got back onto the bus, left him out there and we rode right into camp. Wow!

But from Embry-Riddle I then was assigned to Tyndall Field into gunnery school. Again there's a weeding out, there's a weeding out that took place in Nashville, Tennessee, and then of course when we got to Tyndall you had to go through more classroom work again, but I made it through there. Then I was to be shipped over to Ellington Field in Texas.En route to Ellington Field, we got stopped at New Orleans and we pulled over to a siding. We couldn't go any further because there was an outbreak of meningitis at Ellington Field. So we had about a five day stay over in New Orleans and I got to see the whole town of New Orleans. I tell you that's a jumping place. I highly recommend it to anyone.

We got to Ellington Field finally, we were spending just a few days there, and I got assigned to San Angelo, Texas to a bombardier school, not navigation school, bombardier school. You take what the Army gives you. And again there's classroom work you're doing everything -- I made it, and I got -- that was January 15th of '44. I got my wings and I also got my commission as a second lieutenant in the U.S. Army Air Corps. And by the way, while there we did have navigation. You had to do this. So I was -- the only part of navigation that we did not get exposed to which a navigator would, that would have been the sextant.

Other than that, why, we did everything that a navigator would do as far as being able to give directions to where the pilot is supposed to go. Then I had a 15 day leave, came home and celebrated with my folks; of course, my intended as well. We were not married yet and I didn't intend to because you didn't know what the future would hold because I was going into combat then. Shipped on then to Plant Park in Tampa, Florida.

Plant Park is not a park. Plant Park is actually the stadium in which the Cincinnati Reds would work out for their spring training. So tents were set up all over the field, and we lived in the tents and were just waiting for assignment. Which in about five days, why then we were assigned to RTU training, which is Replacement Training Unit, that's what the RTU means, at Drew Field in Tampa, Florida.

Drew Field today is now the International Airport of Tampa. We got into B17's -- worked up a crew and I was part of that crew. We did the required number of training missions and et cetera. This was at night, day, whatever. And then we completed that, and we got the orders to be ready to be shipped out to overseas.

I was yanked off that crew for some reason or another. I guess they must have felt that I had more than average intelligence and decided to put me in the program, the radar program, this was when radar was in its infancy, and I was shipped to Boca Raton, Florida and started training. And this was -- they were developing a new technique for bombing. Many times the target is cloud covered, but radar can penetrate through the clouds and you can be able to detect your targets. There's may be an outline of a river or whatever. There were various points and et cetera that you can work it through.

But then you're working -- the radar works the rate part of the approach to the target or when to drop the bombs. But then the bombardier, he zeroes in on a point and he tracks. And so the ______was synchronized bombing technique because you are working in conjunction; two people, the bombardier and the mickey man, who is the radar man, are working together in order to drop the bombs on the targets. So this is the training that we were involved in.

And so we got through that program. By the way, Lowell Tope was with me. I still hadn't lost him yet. And he also in the meantime had gotten married to a lovely young girl in St. Petersburg, Florida. I was at the wedding. It was truly nice. We were still together.

It was at that point where we parted. Lowell went off and I was shipped into Langley Field. Why I was shipped there, I have no idea but I was there and I was just sitting on my hands and just waiting. And it took me about eight days or better and finally I was assigned to a crew as a bombardier. I have no reason -- I had no -- I just don't know why. Maybe something had happened to the bombardier. Maybe he got ill or whatever. But he was off of that crew and I replaced him.

From there we flew to Bangor, Maine; Bangor Maine to Gander, Newfoundland. We got socked in Newfoundland because of fog for about ten days but then we managed to get out of Newfoundland and flew to the Azores. From the Azores we flew to Marrakech,, Morocco; from Morocco we went to Tunisia, then from Tunisia we went to Catania, Sicily. From Catania we flew the aircraft to Joya, Italy. And there we remained sitting on our hands again waiting for assignment because we were now a replacement unit.

We were only there a couple of days and then we got -- this is war. In the dead of night practically you could say that we flew the aircraft and landed at Amendola, which is located between Foggia and Macedonia in Italy. So we got on -- the -- the trucks took us onto the base. And we first of all went into the squadron office and we were then introduced to the C.O. He gave us orders and et cetera. And so the next point was after interrogation and that bit, why, he says, You can take any one of that row of empty tents. We looked at one another, and then we learned shortly thereafter that that squadron had been wiped out on their mission just that -- just that morning, just that day. They had cleaned out the tents and took out the personal effects of the officers and we just walked into some empty tents with our gear.

That was really a revelation. That was truly a revelation to us of what combat was like. The captain was made a brand-new captain. He was a survivor to an extent and it was not a mission he flew on, so he was a survivor of the 20th Squadron, which we were assigned to. And -- so he was our C.O. for the 20th Squadron. My first mission was on August 31st of 1944 and this was from the 31st of August to the 3rd of September. We had flights that we were going to Ploiesti. And we were there in order to pick up the POWs because Romania had decided to break away from the fascists and the Russians were coming along the way as well.

So we were there to pick up the POWs. There's a little bit of history here that not many people are aware of, that there were about eleven hundred prisoners, POWs there. They were aided by a Romania princess. Her name was Catherine Caradja and she used her influence at that time and her resources first to keep the prisoners from ever going into Germany to the Stalinites. Kept them in Romania. Secondly, she also used her own resources to make life more bearable to the American POWs. She was a strong anti-communist. For some years after the war, why, she was finally able to escape from Romania and she remained in the U.S until the climate changed.

It was only in 1991 that she finally returned to Romania. My first combat mission took place then -- after that -- I also meant to mention that the first flight to Ploiesti, we landed -- I tell you, it was something at the airport. There were all these POWs lined up along side the runways out in the field. I was afraid we were going to run into these guys. They are just waiting. As soon as the aircraft stops and it sort of just pulls over, they were all ordered to line up and the doors were opened up to allow them to go in. And who is the first guy to get in that plane? The young man from the west side of Cleveland who was in the bombardier class immediately behind me.

His first mission over Ploiesti he got shot down. He was the first guy. I said, You lucky stiff, I said, you're going home. (Laughter.) I hadn't even had my first combat mission yet at that point. I was happy for him, though. We embraced. To him it was so great for him to see a face that he could recognize. I don't know what you call that, fate or whatever. But nevertheless, my first combat mission was on September 5.

That was -- we bombed a railroad bridge in Budapest. But on September 10th I had a great experience. We were bombing an oil refinery in Vienna, and Vienna has -- had 198 flat gun batteries around it, and boy I tell you they ____.

What had happened on that particular mission is two bombs hung up in the bomb bay, and you can't land with anything like that. So it was my responsibility -- I would strap on an oxygen bottle which had about eight to ten minutes of oxygen supply in it so it could be portable. And I got into the bomb bay. The bomb bay doors were open, and there was a catwalk in that bomb bay which was about eight inches wide. And I -- of course, I also had my parachute on as well just in case, and there's these two bombs sitting there. They were still in the racks. So I had to go through the unstuck procedure and get them lined up properly through there and et cetera.

So then we just peeled away. But all during this time, you're fighter bait because when you have an aircraft with the bombs stuck like this, well the orders are that plane pulls away from the formation and you are stuck out and you're fighter bait. Fortunately nothing like that occurred because I -- I didn't see it of course but I had to assume that by this time the fighter -- our own personal fighter escort arrived on the scene again to catch us on the way back from the target to escort us back safely to our base.

But I was able to get them straightened out and got back into my seat there, looked down to see whether there's a clear enough area and I just let go of the bombs. I watched them go down, and they just popped out in an open field and injured no one at all. But then onto September 13th, that was the most horrific raid that I've ever been on. I'd been in some bad ones afterwards, but it was nothing, nothing at all like this.

This is going to Vleck-Hammer North Oil Refinery. And there's a group ahead of us that are going into the target. We were coming right after them and that flak was something. It was just surrounding everything. And here -- the aircraft just exploded into the formation and five planes were just blown right out of the sky. And they deduced what had occurred was just as the bomb released, the flak that was shot up at the aircraft, why, it exploded at the same time with the bombs and that just lit up the sky.

I just saw a B-17 just burst apart and look just like a hay stack. You're looking for parachutes and you're not seeing anything. There's just nothing. At that point, I've got to tell you (starts crying). I didn't think I would do this. I was -- in all honesty I was saying Hail Mary's and swearing like hell at the same time because I knew I had to go through that. But we did and we got them, got peppered like hell and our aircraft was hit many times.

As a matter of fact, when we landed, why, the crew chief on the ground had discovered that the nose cone from one of the flaks, the shell from the flak, had penetr Ated the wing between the number three and number four engines themselves. Fortunately we made it okay. On September 18th, why, it was my first lone wolf mission. This is a new twist that the Air Force decided -- that they decided they would try to play. And that is the group goes to a regular specific target, but then we would be taking off in the dead of night at all odd hours and the planes would be going alone, not in formation this time. No escort and we were going in train.

We would be separated three to ten minutes apart. The idea was that we would be going into the enemy territory and the air raid sirens would be going constantly down there, and this was to break the moral of the people that are there, and at the same time we were going for a specific target. And my first lone wolf mission was over _____ in Yugoslavia and that was going for the marshalling yards. I did want to mention as well that on these missions we bombed the targets, but at the same time we also would be dropping propaganda leaflets.

And these were written in the language of the country that we were going to, whether it be Yugoslavia, be it Italy, or Austria Germany, that would be the Germany language. Hungry of course would be Hungarian. Well, I had taken German in school and I was fairly fluent with it, so I would read to the crew exactly the message that we were sending to the people that were in the area that we were bombing. And this was to counter whatever Goebels was giving to them in his propaganda speeches. But I had a lot of lone missions that were --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What exactly was being said in the propaganda leaflets?

sp.speaker: Raymond E. Tuwalski
sp.p: As far as in the propaganda leaflets, the actual status of where actually the front lines were, which towns were taken. And actually at times we had where a division of troops was actually captured. It was truthful, it was actually truthful.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. You can go back. I'm sorry I interrupted.

sp.speaker: Raymond E. Tuwalski
sp.p: That's okay. But I'd say -- where are we?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Lone wolf missions.

sp.speaker: Raymond E. Tuwalski
sp.p: Yes, there we are again. All right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you did these lone wolf missions, would you all be bombing the same target if you got separated?

sp.speaker: Raymond E. Tuwalski
sp.p: The same target. Usually it would be the same target, that is correct. There was only one raid that we went -- people that were going out, they went to three different targets. One was going to Glywitch (phonetic). We of course were going to Vleck-Hammer. I can't recall where the third party was going to. They were going to some target in Poland. That's where they were going. Other than that, we would be going to one specific target. These were all no fighter escort and you're not flying in formation because if you are together in formation, why, then there's more fire power to protect yourself.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the greatest separation of the planes then?

sp.speaker: Raymond E. Tuwalski
sp.p: The greatest separation between them would be ten minutes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Ten minutes?

sp.speaker: Raymond E. Tuwalski
sp.p: So ten minutes -- if you're talking ten minutes, your thing is 20 miles. If it's three minutes, well then it's six miles, or at times it may even be less. But we were never, just never, together.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So the idea was to lengthen the time of attack --

sp.speaker: Raymond E. Tuwalski
sp.p: Oh, definitely. It --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- lots of people on the ground?

sp.speaker: Raymond E. Tuwalski
sp.p: Oh, God, yes. We had some missions where we would take off it would be 10 o'clock at night. We wouldn't be coming back until 7 something in the morning because these missions were quite lengthy -- or even 9 o'clock. As I said, our missions we'd be gone -- like we had one particular one, of all things we went out to Vienna Vloridsdorf Refinery on a lone wolf mission and the entire 15th Air Force, I mean that's the whole Air Force, all the wings, for some little old crappy town called Mirabal, Yugoslavia -- going into the marshalling yards.

And the only reason they went there is because -- all of a sudden there were a lot of cars being gathered together there. They were going to get the troops from the Balkan area, the German troops out of the Balkan area, and get them back over into Germany to help fight, you know, whatever front they were required to. And so I guess the 15th Air Force really must have done their job because they were never able to get the troops through there. So they were trapped and the Russians got them, got most of them. Do you want me to go on here?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes,

sp.speaker: Raymond E. Tuwalski
sp.p: At the end of September, why, there were torrential rains and they went on even into October. It was at that time that the -- I was again shipped over to a school in Bari, Italy. I was given orders to go there and to learn additional techniques in this synchronic bombing because there was another radar set more advanced than the one we had been training in. It was at that time that I stayed at the Oriental Hotel during that training period. And I discovered the little village of Cosenza which was about maybe 15, 20 miles east of Bari, Italy. Bari is right on the coast of the Adriatic Sea.

I discovered that there was a Polish contingent there, actually was a Polish hospital, Polish First General Hospital. My father coming originally from Poland, why, I decided, hey, I'm going over there and maybe someone came from my dads's village. I had a vehicle at my disposal, so I drove over there and started roaming around and here was a YWCA.

It was a two-story building. I walked into there and it was for the officers, where they could lounge around a bit. I went on down to the second level, and there were nurses up there and they were playing bridge. Here I'm -- I go over to sit down and I'm watching them play bridge. And of course they looked me over because I don't have a Polish uniform. They recognized I was American. I introduced myself and I told them the reason I was there. I said, If you don't mind, I'll sit and watch how you're playing this game.

It was kind of odd to see them betting in the Polish language, betting in Polish. I got to be friendly with them and told them the purpose of why I was there. So one of the nurses took me then over to -- into the hospital area and introduced me to the superintendent of nurses and her name happened to be Eulainsco (phonetic.) And I told her the reason I was there, so she went to inquire if anybody was from the area, the village of Mitzco where my dad came from, and nobody did. Many of them didn't even know a village like that existed in Poland.

So I went down a dead end, but I got friendly with the people. And -- so then I returned back again to the base. I was sitting at the officers' mess eating and here word came out that the 300 -- the Second Bomb Group was going to celebrate their 300th mission and it was going to be taking place on November 11th, which would be Armistice Day. But they were looking for -- if they could get some guests in, young ladies, et cetera. They didn't want any--the camp followers. If anyone came from the town, it would have to be someone who was rather elegant to dress up the occasion.

I failed to mention something that's very important. When I was en route to Bari to go to school for the first time, I was taken there by a captain to show me the ropes. And en route, why, we stopped off at a cluster of buildings which were just before the town of Bari and it was called Geo-van-netza (phonetic). And at that cluster of buildings I was introduced to some American ladies, and this was in a UNO Station, United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation. These were ladies there who were doing their services.

And inside these buildings were cribs, little beds and all these little children are in there. Just wall to wall and just stacked together. It went from room to room and each one of these rooms were just loaded with these cribs and these little children. Some are just laying down. They are just little tiny babies. And others are just months old. I didn't see anyone there that could have been any more than 18 months or maybe 24 months in there.

I said, What's going on here? And here I discovered that all of these children are the babies or the children of partisans from Yugoslavia. And what would occur is the partisans would decoy or whatever -- they would attack troops, they would kill them, et cetera. And of course the German commanders knew where it all came from and, why, they would go in there and just wipe out the village. Kill everybody in that village. They wouldn't kill the children. They took them and they would just take them out in the woods and drop the kids off, the little babies off in the woods.

Of course, any of the other underground partisans that were left, why, they would find these children, and then they would take them off to the Yugoslav post, and then they were distributed across the Adriatic and they were brought to this place that had three buildings, room after room, room after room after room with all these babies in every room. Holy cow.

So when I was driving myself, once I got to know the ropes, because I would be going to the school in between flying missions. That's about a 120 mile drive, by the way, around my base to drive to Bari, Italy. But I would stay there for a day or two and then I'd come back and fly missions, so on and so forth. But every time I drove down, I loaded myself down with every goody I could have for these kids.

I used to give them packages of these lemon drops. I'd go in there and -- it was -- the look on these kids -- it'd be just like you'd have a nest of baby birds and their mouths are just wide open. You're just popping these lemon drops. The kids are standing up and they're all shouting because I'm coming in there. I was like Santa Claus. Those that could speak -- I learned one word from them and it was Gesgaval (phonetic)
(Side 1 ends.)
(Side 2 starts.)

sp.speaker: Raymond E. Tuwalski
sp.p: Wow. What a feeling that was. And of course for the ladies -- I'd get a free meal out of it as well. I had access to getting things from the black market because everything over there was barter. I didn't smoke that much and had candy bars up the kazoo and all of that. And I would go in and I would trade this stuff and I would get nylon stockings, and nylon stockings were very important, so I would go around and give these ladies the nylon stockings as well I would get a free meal out of it.

It didn't cost me, so to speak. But that's what went on. However, getting back now when I'm back to one of these sessions at the school in Bari and it's revealed they are going to have this 300th mission party and they need girls. So I inquired of the special service officer, I say, Now, I may have access to some but I would need transportation. And he said, I'll get you transportation to anywhere you want to go. I said, You really mean it? And he said, Yes. So I said, Well, there's a possibility I may have some nurses and they are from another country. I don't know how many. But I may; I'm not certain. But then I also have some American ladies as well. Americans? Where do you get American nurses?

So the C.O. happened to have overheard this and he said, Put that kid off flying status, which I no longer was. So I had four days in which I couldn't fly any missions. And my assignment for the group was that I was to go around and negotiate for these ladies and come back and make sure that they had them. In fact, I went down there and I came back to this First Polish General Hospital at the worst time you could ever imagine because it was during that time that the uprising had taken place in Warsaw and the Russian troops are standing at the east side of Batolla River which is right at Warsaw and they refuse to go across to help the Poles who are having this uprising against the Germans.

They just stood there and never crossed in order to aid the Poles. And so the Poles were decimated. So they were in mourning, and here I'm inviting them to come to this party. And so they are in mourning. I said, Oh, my. I pressed my case and pressed my case with Eulainsco even to the extent that finally it got -- I must've been a good salesman because she then led me into the office of the commandant, a Polish colonel, a surgeon. And I spoke with him then. Good thing that my command of the Polish language was pretty fairly decent then. And I pressed my case, and he turned around and looked at Ula and he says, -- he gave her the number of ladies. I was astounded because here I was getting 16 nurses. Can you imagine.

I said, We need transportation, which was aerial transportation not by bus or any land conveyance. So I got the 16 girls, you know. And I relied on Ula which ones they were going to be. And then of course I went back -- I'd already stopped off at the Uno Station. You can just never figure women, truly you can't imagine it. Because I'm telling them about this party, you know sitting down eating. And one said, Would you please wait?

Do you know these girls came back out and they had evening gowns. They'd gone over to -- from America into a combat area and they brought along evening gowns. You figure. Holy cow. So I said, Geeze, that's fantastic, so all right. Then I came back to the base and I said, I do have them. It was agreed upon. And I said, Now I need this transportation. So okay. So again I fly in missions but I'm flying milk runs this time because I had to go back out. But in the meantime when I did go, why, and we took a -- it was an ambulance that we took with us. And so I rode with the ambulance driver non stop all the way down there. And initially I took care of the American women. And what had happened was they had a B-17 that flew down over to the airport at Bari. I picked the American girls up. Of course we'd made arrangements for their accommodations as well.

And all of the hospitals -- the squadron -- our bomb group was comprised of four squadrons and each squadron had a hospital. Well, no one was sick. They just pulled them all out of the hospitals and the hospital beds that were there, they were made available, you know, for the guests that were coming in and anything else that we -- we gave up our own quarters as well, my buddy and I. So I took care of -- as soon as they took off from Bari with the American girls, then I drove down and we got another vehicle and over to the First Polish General Hospital, picked up all of the Polish nurses and drove out to the base. I needed two planes. So they came back with two B-17's, and they -- the gals were really excited being able to fly in an American bomber.

Inquisitive? Holy cow. But what a time I had. (Laughter) I had this table with all these nurses, was a huge one, and I was the interpreter. I got to dance only once. And other than that -- when the guys discovered that I had access to all these girls, there was a sign up sheet. The end result was that I had the guy's name and then when all the girls were there lined up and I'd just call the guy's name and I'd take a Polish nurse and I'd hand her over to the guy. But that was a great party. It truly was a great party.

But then -- shortly thereafter, well, then I had a flying mission afterwards -- and they stayed at our quarters, so we took all of our duds over to the officers' mess and that's where we changed clothes and left everything there and waited for breakfast. And then -- after that for the briefing for the mission and then we took off for the mission. Shortly thereafter, why, I had another mission. And I truly have gotten way ahead of myself about another situation. That was when I had the -- was with the crew and I had to go into the school, why, the crew that I came across the pond with, why, they kept flying missions and here I was going to school, so they were way ahead of me as far as missions. In the meantime I had become friendly with three other guys, and they were from another squadron of our group. They were from, I think they were from the 96th Squadron.

One of them was Arnold Prowgushski (phonetic) and the other one was David Ismen and a Stan Smorag (phonetic). And I guess because in a sense that would be three of us Poles and Ismen was a Jewish boy. And so we got -- we played pinochle always at the officers' club. So this was going on night after night, either that or I'd be writing letters to Dorothy or listening to Axis Sally letting us -- telling us what our next mission was going to be. A real tragedy -- on October 17th, why, we lost Arnold and David. They were on mission and they were over this target at Vleck-Hammer again, this horrible target because that was loaded with flak guns.

And the plane that was on -- Arnold was the squadron lead and the plane that was on his wing got hit by flak. And when it got hit by flak, why, it went in and the wing of the wingman's plane went right into the waist of Arnold's plane and the plane just broke in two -- Arnold's did. And they just plummeted down and never got out.

So here Stan was the bombardier and he was sick. He had a real bad cold so he wasn't flying. He was just beside himself. Talk about a guy just crying his eyes out. He comes to me and he says, Ray, I can't stay alone. I can't stay alone. Here I was staying in the quarter with my -- the crew that I was always flying with. And I felt sorry for the guy and I said, I can't. I said, You're in another squadron. I'm in the 20th Squadron and you are in the 96th. He said, I'm going to kill myself because I can't stand it. I said, Well, tell you what, let's go over to group headquarters. So I went into the group headquarters and told them what the heck was going on and et cetera. They took one look at him and all of that, and the C.O. said, Son, you two bunk together. Take care of him. So that's -- I moved out.

Of course, that made the officers in the crew that I was in madder than hell but I stood my ground. Truly you had to see the situation. This guy was really in a bad way. So we got together at this point. And then lo and behold, I'm alone -- I'm still flying with my crew, and on the 13th of November, which is just two days after our party, this mission that I was on, why, it was another lone wolf mission. And we had on board then a war correspondent for Yank magazine. His name was George Barrett. Our target was Vleck-Hammer North again.

And we were as usual going in train, minutes and et cetera apart. As I understand it, we were the third aircraft in that train. And as we were going, why, we were at high altitude. We were either at 27,000 or 29,000 feet. And fortunately when you take off and et cetera -- and if you go on this long haul like this, why, the pilot -- you go on auto pilot, so I turned on the switch for my bomb sight which would be not for the sight itself, but for the other -- it was for the see-win gyro (phonetic) which is utilized for automatic pilot.

The pilot then just cages in on it, but I have to have the switch on so it's running. So we were on automatic pilot going en route to the target. However, when we were just I'd say a half hour or so away from the target, why, then I would turn on the bomb sight itself because there's another gyro in that particular one too, which they all work in conjunction one with another. And here the thing just wouldn't go at all. And I looked at the thermometer outdoors and it was 60 degrees below zero and that bomb sight was frozen. It wasn't working.

And would you believe the target was clear? Oh, it was clear. And somehow or another a plane that was supposed to be ahead of us never made it there, got caught in the lights, in search lights, and just couldn't get out of it. I don't know what happened to the other one. But we're going in now and I can see that target. So we had the mickey man on board, and so he took over the rad control which is very accurate, truly is very accurate with the newer radar bomb -- or radar set, the APQ 13 radar set. I then took care of track. And boy I tracked that sucker and I was running on that target. And I have a feeling about when bombs should let go and I'm working with the mickey man because he's counting to me and I'm counting back to him.

And I said, You let these things go now or I'm going to salvo these things. He said, Wait a minute, wait a minute. Trust me, you know. I said, Okay. And Byron Martin was the mickey man and he let go, and I could follow these things through and we traced it right through Vleck-Hammer. The fires that we started in that place were unbelievable. So we truly hit that target, but we were hit. We lost two engines over the target and we were losing altitude then. So we just swung out and we just were limping along going lower, and the pilot decided he'd better get behind the enemy lines which would be getting over more toward Russian territory. And we -- so we were going along pretty well in through there and we were drawing close to Budapest, and there I got a ring side seat at the siege of Budapest.

It was fantastic. The fire power that was going. The Russians had these patusha (phonetic) rockets and all the artillery and you could see the entire horizon just blazing, just red blazing. And then you see this -- you are looking down below and all these shells are landing on the target in and around Budapest. And here all of a sudden we're in flak. So we got the heck out of there. But we were beginning to lose altitude. We couldn't make it, so we started dumping anything that was heavy out of there. That meant taking the bomb sight, heaving it overboard, all the machine guns, all the ammunition, anything. We were just throwing everything overboard in order to lighten the load of the aircraft.

And when we were going through Yugoslavia up through the Dolomite mountains, why, we were at an altitude which is lower than the mountain peaks. And at that time the question was are they going to just take off and jump, you know, parachute, just leave the plane and jump? But we all took a head count and we all decided we were going to stay with the plane. So I said, Hey, there's a river down there. If it's a river, it's a valley. So I could see the river and so we just followed it on through. Thank God that there was no island with a huge peak in there that we would have run head-on into. But we broke out then over the Dalmatian coast, and we were heading then for the island of Vish (phonetic) which was held by the partisans. There was a runway there that we could land on.

And it began to snow. Snowing like bloody hell. And so he couldn't -- and he was making a pass with the island, and Vish is a pear-shaped island and at the point of the pear that's where you start the runway. But at the blunt part of the pear of the shape of the island, why, there's these mountains. You make one pass. If you don't make it, you can be splashed into the mountains. The pilot was afraid to take the risk and he decided we're going to try to go to -- get as close as possible to the Italian coast. I could actually see from where I was sitting in the front because I'm in the Plexiglass nose of the B-17, and I could actually see planes taking off from the airfield.

But we'd already keyed in with mayday at that point that we're not going to make it. And so then we got in the position for ditching procedure, and so -- Peterson was the pilot and, boy, he made as soft a landing for ditching as you ever wanted to see. There was hell to pay because I went into the radio room and that's where everyone was clustered in. There was only the pilot, the co-pilot, and the navigator, and the crew chief that were up in the front at that point.

I was in the radio room and I was in charge of all the people there, and I wanted to make certain that George Barrett was well taken care of. We took all cushioned pads et cetera, wrapped it around him in order to make certain that he be safe. And I'm the guy that's up against the bulkhead and everybody's in front of me. When we hit the water, why, the shock was really great. And all the heads went bobbing in together and I got smashed in the face. George Barrett just flew straight on up and his head got knocked up against the gun mount. And the radio man, Nochay (phonetic) why, his head hit the radio, so he got cut in the forehead. So we start pouring out of there and I'm the last guy out. I made sure that George Barrett was out there first.

And I started calling the guys, Who's going up next to get the heck out of there? And when it was my turn to get out, why, I was already waist deep in water in the aircraft. I tried to get out and I couldn't make it because I was so water logged. I was really soaking wet. And I went towards the waist and I figured, geeze, maybe I'm better off just going out the waist door or the waist window. And I figured, Hey, if I go back there, the center of gravity is going to change with this thing and it's liable to do something else, so I'll do something else. So I go back in the radio room and I stayed and I just got my feet -- one foot up on the mickey table and the other foot up on the radio table and I was just spread eagle that way, and I was able to lift myself up and get out to the opening.

The -- I got my elbows across the hatch and lifted myself up out of there. Now I'm straddling the fuselage of the plane. Everybody is nervous as hell because the dinghies are out and all, and I'm supposed to go into the right-hand dinghy of the aircraft. I said, Just wait a minute. And I had my--what do they call it?--it's a crush 50 mission hat, I just straightened it up on my head. So I slid down the fuselage onto the wing and then I just walked right over--right into the dinghy. And so we pull away from the aircraft because that thing's going to go down. And so we pulled away.

In the meantime, I'm looking across there and there's some Italian fishing boats heading out in our direction. So I -- I'm in charge of the dinghy. I get a head count of the guys. I'm calling roll. I know everybody that's supposed to be there. So I said, Martin, you know, but I don't see Martin. Everybody what was in the dinghy raised their head. I said, Where the hell's Martin? Here one of the fellows is pointing, and I look and here Martin's in the water. I said, What the hell you doing there? And he said, I'm all right. I'm all right. I said, Get your ass in here. He says, I'm all right. I'm all right. I'm like, Like hell. Holy cow, don't tell me. I'm in water up to here. You can't tell me -- I've got to go in there now and get him because he was a case of shock.

That's exactly what was wrong with Byron. So I went and popped my Mae West because I hadn't even done that yet. They was just still flat. So I pulled the two handles on the Mae West and it inflated; into the water I go. I asked one of the men that was in the dinghy with me, I said, Well, you get ahold of his harness and we're going to get him in here. And all the while all you got of him was, I'm all right. I'm all right. I'm all right. Just a litany of "I'm all rights." And so I don't know where I got the strength, but I grabbed ahold with the left hand the rope on the edge of the dinghy, and I got my right hand with the parachute harness that he was wearing and I got underneath his crotch and I don't know where I got it but I lifted his butt straight up out of the water like this and I said, Pull. So then we just shoved him inside of the dinghy.

Now I am thoroughly wet by this time because -- and I get in there. And so we're in the dinghy and then the Italian fishing boats came along side, one of them did. We all piled into it. So -- and we say, Macedonia. That would be where the docks were. And here comes a rescue boat. It's one of the British rescue boats that comes out. And we're witnessing this thing come along. And they got the bright idea that they were going to tow this aircraft in. And I'm yelling -- we're pulling along side of them. I'm yelling and I said, Don't do it. It's loaded with water. It's going to be a sea anchor if you try to pull it. They're not paying a bit of attention to me. They went and they wrapped a huge line around the tail end of this thing and they're going to pull it. Unfortunately, there was a guy -- one of the crewman was on deck there along the railing. And when they started pulling, all of a sudden you can see it ain't going to work, you know, and they're going to get sucked under with this thing, or something horrible is going to happen, or it's going to capsize on them, their vessel would capsize.

So they're -- so he took an ax over there and one swing and he cut that rope just right in two and down went our plane at this point. It took the deep six. So now we're heading back. It's nice and calm. We're headed towards Macedonia. All the while Byron, we've got him propped up against one of the masts of the fishing boat. He's, I'm all right. I'm all right. And here I reach in my pocket, by golly, I've got my cigarette case there. I said, I wonder if the cigarettes are dry. And I pulled it out. It was a cigarette case that Dorothy had given to me. And so I open up the cigarette case. All of them are good.

And the Italian fishermen, they see cigarettes, you know, holy macaroni. So the first thing I did, I walked over there and gave each one of them one, snapped my Zippo lighter and lit the cigarettes for them. Then I walked over and there's Byron, I'm all right. I'm all right. I shoved a cigarette in his mouth and I lit it. When I did that, he shut up. He started smoking. So I gave cigarettes to the rest of the crew. I had three cigarettes left in this thing. It took all three cigarettes to keep him quiet. So when we got there, why, the ambulances were there waiting for us and et cetera to take us over to the hospital area.

All I did, I got my face bashed in, my two front teeth, upper teeth, were all pushed in, and so I was on soft food for awhile afterwards. Other than that I was okay. But that was the extent of it. So we had one day's rest. When I came in, if you want to say this, after I got out of the hospital, they told me I was okay. It was just a matter of me being in early, about an hour or so, and then they released us. I didn't want anything.

All I wanted was sleep. That's all. I got into our hut and I just shucked off my clothes and just went into the sack and I just fell dead away. When I woke up, why, there I see Stan. He's been sitting all the while, he said, just looking at me. Tears were coming out of his eyes. He was so happy that I was there because he said, I don't know what the hell I'd do, you know, if you go. I must've been an anchor for him when we were together.
But we had -- a day after that we had another mission to fly and they do that to make damn sure that you don't lose your nerve.

But Byron, he never flew. I don't know whatever happened to him thereafter. My buddy Tope, he was -- I failed to mention that he ended up in the same bomb group as I was but he was with another squadron. We never -- but he flew that very same lone wolf mission, and they got shot up just as badly. I learned from their crew that, boy, thank God that we did what we did because they were able to see the target because we lit it up like a Christmas tree. And so they all -- they were all going in to wipe out the Vleck-Hammer North, which is a synthetic oil refinery. But they got shot up so badly that they crash landed on the beach or the Adriatic, and they were able to make it back.

Tope was so shook up by it all that he never flew again either and he wound up at a hospital. But he was there at the hospital, but then that's the last I saw of him. When we -- we had this other mission to fly which was just two days after. When we landed, why, we were informed that orders were cut that we could go anywhere now for a rest leave, either Rome, Capri, Naples, wherever you wanted to go. I said, Boy, I'm going. So here the crew is again in a snit about it, why I want to be going when they've got missions to fly.

They said, Good heavens, they said, we've just got about four more missions to go and we're going to have our missions in and we'll be going home. Why, by the time we'd be coming back from rest leave, we'd already be going home. So why do you want to do that? And I looked at them, I said, Look, you guys have been flying those missions while I've been going to school and I still have a long way to go. I said, No. I said, If the Army's giving you something for nothing, you take it, you know. And some of the enlisted men, there were three enlisted men of the crew, they got to thinking about it also. And they said, By God, we're going to go with you, sir, you know. And so we got orders cut and we were going to Rome. It was supposed to have been for five days. Well, we were there but transportation failed us. We ended up we were 19 days in Rome. And I walked all over the streets of Rome. I saw all those historic sites.

In the meantime, just about five blocks -- I was staying at the Savoy Hotel. And the matride of that hotel in the dining room, why, he happened to be also a waiter on the Condese (phonetic) Savoy and he gave me a photograph of him standing between Tyrone Power and Anabella when they were on their honeymoon trip. So I got to talking with him and he spoke excellent English. Really a nice guy.

But about five blocks away from the Savoy Hotel was a hotel which billeted the Polish troops that were on rest leave. And after I'd seen all the sites I wanted to see and all that bit, why, I wondered in -- because the Red Cross was -- also they had good movies going on every day.

So now I walked over to there and I said, Well, maybe somebody over there knows where this town of Lenyetsga(phonetic) is and knows about my folks in Poland. And I walked into there and they all looked at me again and it was just like Castle-machem (phonetic) all over again. So I inquired and a gentleman came up to me and he says, Can I help you? And I said, Yes. So I introduced myself, told him the situation. He said, Well, I'll inquire about it. So in the meantime, he says, What are you doing?

And I told him the situation that I was on rest leave and all. I never talked about the missions or anything of that sort. I was just on rest leave and enjoying the historic sites of Rome. You know Rome? I said, I've been walking all over this place. So he said, I'd like to see it. I just came. So I said, Well, fine. And the gentleman, he turned -- he was a war correspondent. So here we're going and I'm taking on all the sites in Rome. He starts turning around and he wants to look for a ride, for transportation. I said, You're going to miss too much if you're riding. I said, You got to walk this. So I had him walking and God we walked through every -- the Colosseum, the -- just about everything you can imagine, all the fountains, the -- everything imaginable that was there. And in the evenings, that was the only time we took a conveyance and that was that he ordered what he called a deluxishe (phonetic) which happened to be a horse and carriage and a driver, and we'd go to the opera, to the Rome opera. And the Rome opera house, it's an elegant opera house.

One of the rare things about it is the fact, and I don't think to this day unless they've done something with it, but Mussolini's name is in the archway above the stage of the Rome opera house. There we got to see operas. One that I can remember, Cab of the Rustocnia (phonetic) is one. All Mighty was another one. Madame Butterfly was another one that we -- so -- and we always had good box seats. Now, all right. After I returned, why, -- in the meantime I'd received an air medal for the missions that I flew. I guess in recognition to some of the work that I did with the hung up bombs in the bomb bay.

Incidentally that situation developed on another mission and that was a real strange one because the bombs -- we're again stuck out there away from the--our formation, and while my pilot is waiting to see--for me to get those bombs straightened out in the bomb bay. And here again there were two bombs hung up again. And so I got -- I corrected the situation. I got back again into the bomb sight and I'm looking out and I said, my God, there's farms out here. I ain't going to drop these bombs. I've got to find a place where it's nice and clear. And I couldn't at that point.

In the meantime everybody's -- the whole entire crew and the pilot especially is getting nervous. So I -- I said, Now, just wait a minute. I can't drop these bombs. He said, Why can't you drop the bombs? I said, There's people down there. They may be enemies but they're innocent. They have nothing to do with the war, I feel. Why should I just indiscriminately let these bombs go? They might land, God forbid, on a farm house or school house, you name it. So we got to a clearing and here there was a road that I saw. I said -- I was able -- because the aircraft was under my control. And I swung it around and I was going along this road.

And I said, Well, I'm going to bomb the road, so I let the bombs go. And when I let them go, son of a gun, the pilot just wheeled that aircraft around. My head just slammed right into the Plexiglass nose because I'm looking down. I'm trying to see where in the hell these bombs are going. I want to see where they're going to land--where they're going to fall. And so I yell out to the crew, I said, Keep an eye on those bombs. But when he straightened out, I still was able to see, and would you believe there was a vehicle going down a -- it was a military vehicle speeding down the road. And those two bombs, they didn't hit the road, but what they did is they landed and they bracketed the road just exactly where that vehicle was. But I hoped to God that I didn't kill them at this point, but it must've burst their eardrums. I've got to get back again to Rome.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go right ahead. Go back to wherever you need to go back to.

sp.speaker: Raymond E. Tuwalski
sp.p: Okay. So while in Rome this time with the -- with Dr. Klenshinski (phonetic) who was the Polish war correspondent, he said I would like to invite you to go with us to the Vatican. I said, Yeah, but I'm an American. He said, Well, we have an audience with the Pope. I said, Wow. Yeah, but I'm American. It doesn't matter at all. He says, We've got a bus. I've got a place for you on the bus. So there was a bus that picked us up and drove us over to the grounds of the Vatican. We got off of that and we went into the Sistine Chapel because that was where the audience then was being held with the Pope.

This was a private audience with the Pope. No one else but the Polish troops. The Polish troops had their chaplain who happened to have been a bishop. And so we all sung Polish songs, you know, to the Pope. I didn't recognize all of them, but I gave what I could. And after it was over with, why, they all got in line up towards Pope Pius XII. And so I just stood back. I'm not going to get in line. It's these people; not me. And so but then Iganus (phonetic) came over to me.

He said, You must come. I said, Hey, this is for your troops. No, you come with me. So I went over there and I was tailing Charlie then over to meet the Pope. He looked at me and he says, You are British? I said, No, Your Excellency. I'm American. He must've thought I was because I was wearing an Eisenhower jacket at that particular time that I'd had made -- had a courtier make for me. So I said, No, Your Excellency. I am American. Then I went to kneel down to kiss his ring, and he says, No, please, you know. And he just stood up and he just held my hands and, It was so nice of you to come.

That was, wow. That was extremely ___ to be there and just to have the brief, you know, conversation with the Pope, Pope Pius XII. To me he was a very saintly man. Say what you will, there are so many thoughts about him, Jews especially what their feelings are. But he was one of the driving forces if you look into the CC Underground where he got so many of the -- priests especially then -- a lot of Jews became Christians, et cetera, and their lives were saved. You can't do it all for everyone. It's just impossible. But I tell you, he was a very saintly man. I was very impressed. To me that was the highlight, truly the highlight of my stay in Rome at that time. But now when we got back to the base there was really a shocker, because the very second next mission that Peterson flew and the crew that I'd ditched in the Adriatic, the ones who were so eager to continue on flying as versus taking that rest leave, they were shot down. All of them ended up in prison except two.

Lt. Phillips who was the bombardier who took my spot that I normally would have had in the crew -- or if I'd been the mickey man, well, I'd been in prison. I'd been a POW. But if I'd been the bombardier and jumped out, why, he's the one that made it back. And he had to fight with the--along side the partisans in order to make it back. But before I got out and flew my missions, he did make it back in time and I got to see him. Then I -- my -- already by that time I'd got to be a First Lieutenant. And I'd been receiving a lot of oak leaf clusters, you know, which is the same thing as saying I got another air medal.

I wound up in the service there with three oak leaf clusters. But on January 16th I was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross. That was with the success I had on that Vleck-Hammer mission that we ditched. So that was awarded to me for the work that I had done. My last mission was on February 23rd. That was to a town call Warglug (phonetic) in Austria. Immediately after I landed, why, I had a cablegram sent to Dorothy to tell her my missions are done. I'm coming home and let's get married. And -- but we finally took off. We took off in what looked like was a commercial aircraft. But we first of all landed in Bermuda overnight and then from Bermuda we landed over state side. So okay, the orders are cut for me now to go Camp Atterbury but I did not pass the physical to go because I was underweight. I was six foot tall, and I never realized what combat does to you, because I weighed only 112 pounds. Lord knows only what I weighed before I got to Miami where we finally landed. But I had to remain there and was off, oh God, it was several different -- when they -- I had to be up to 125 pounds.

Finally I was released and I was shipped to Camp Atterbury, Indiana and from there I was given a release then of 21 day leave. I got home -- and I'm sitting up front now with the cab driver. Four people are squeezed up into the back and we're having this conversation. They said, Your folks know you're coming? And I says, Well, they know I'm coming but they don't know I'm here. And they said, Wow, that's strange. You should've let -- I said, Well, I didn't even let my fiancee know that I've finally reached town. I thought I'd wait until I got home and then I would give her a call after I got home. So wow. So they said, This is something. So they said to the cab driver, Look, when we get to this young man's house, we don't want to leave. We want to see what's going to go on.

So we arrived and the house is dark. Well, I always knew that they kept the side door opened. In the meantime -- I failed to mention that I'd picked up a dog when I was through RTU training, a little cocker spaniel that had flown with us on -- and then I shipped him back home when I was ready to go overseas. And so I opened up that side door and out jumps Flipper. He was out -- he was peeing all over the driveway because he was so dog gone happy to see me and et cetera. And so I picked him up after he got done peeing because I didn't want him to pee all over my uniform.

He was licking me all over the face. And so then I shoved the dog back into the house again and closed the door. And I walked out to the cab and I said, I'm sorry to disappoint you, I says, but it looks like my folks are not at home. And, Ohhhh. And so I said, Don't worry about it. But they all helped me haul all my baggage into the house and then they all left. So I decided I'd go to the neighbors, and these were all spinster ladies living there with their parents. I rang the doorbell.

They opened the door and they were so shocked and were hugging me all over. And they says, Do you know where your folks are and your intended? We were supposed to be there, but we gave, you know, our gifts in advance to your folks. I said, Oh, they're having a shower party for my intended. And they were the most surprised of all I think because I walked into the door and all these ladies are in there chattering away, and they all looked at me and they just kept chattering away all over again. And you could read in their mind, It's their shower party. Ray should be here. Never realizing that I'd just arrived.

But my brother was, he was working behind the bar. He vaulted over that doggone bar and was just hugging me, my dad as well was hugging. And I looked across and Dorothy was there opening a gift and she just scattered that, I don't know what it was, but she just was just beside herself composed -- I guess she didn't want me to see her crying, you know, that I was there.
